nodes.label: Sale & Purchase Agreement (SPA)
nodes.rationale: The SPA is the terminal milestone: it is the executed contract of sale, and the 10% sum is due on signing less the booking fee.

nodes.label: Booking Leakage
nodes.rationale: A substantial share of post-launch bookings quietly falls apart before an executed SPA, holding units off market for 6 to 12 weeks and accruing sunk marketing, commission and legal cost.

nodes.label: PJD Regency v Tribunal Tuntutan Pembeli Rumah (2021)
nodes.rationale: The Federal Court ruled statutory liquidated ascertained damages for late delivery run from the date the booking fee is collected, not SPA signature; in that case booking to SPA took about 64 days, so every stalled week counts against the delivery clock.

nodes.label: Sales And Finance Tension
nodes.rationale: Sales fears stricter pre-qualification will dampen booking velocity and kill launch momentum; Finance knows unweighted bookings are not cash. Mortar resolves this without throttling front-end sales, surfacing stalls in a daily queue instead of imposing rigid gates.

nodes.label: Centralized Case Workspace (/bookings/:id)
nodes.rationale: Every unit booking gets a case dossier with a timestamped auditable event log recording when events occurred, when Mortar learned of them, who reported them and who verified them.

nodes.label: Loan And Legal Parallel Tracks
nodes.rationale: Loan and legal workflows run on separate overlapping tracks: a bank delay must not halt preliminary legal file preparation, and one bank rejection must not mark a multi-application booking as failed.

nodes.label: Unknown Is Visible (10+ Days No Event)
nodes.rationale: A live booking with no confirmed event for ten or more days shows as unknown, preventing stale cases from masquerading as healthy pipeline.
nodes.norm_label: unknown is visible (10+ days no event)

nodes.label: Waiting On
nodes.rationale: Daily triage reduces to four questions: where the unit is, what blocks it, who must move next, and what that move is. Every open case names the party it waits on, what that party owes, and the next move, on the table and the case page alike.

nodes.label: Ask Mortar
nodes.rationale: An embedded assistant that answers natural-language questions from any page, reading the live bookings snapshot with five read-only tools and returning grounded answers with booking citations. It never modifies data or makes credit, loan or legal decisions.

nodes.label: Ask Mortar Five Read-Only Tools
nodes.rationale: find_bookings, get_case, get_my_queue, get_forecast_summary and search_playbooks ground every answer; citations link exclusively to cases returned by those tools in the same turn.

nodes.label: Ask Mortar Boundary
nodes.rationale: Read-only operation, no operational authority, untrusted context isolation for buyer/banker/solicitor bodies, verifiable citations, 503 safe fallback to scripted answers, and no logging of keys or message contents. On Gemini's free tier prompts may be retained for training, so Ask Mortar is restricted to simulated data until an enterprise agreement.

nodes.label: High-Density Ledger Design
nodes.rationale: A white ground with 1px hairline-separated cards at 6px radius; gradients, floating drop shadows and glassmorphism are banned. Geist for interface text, Geist Mono for unit codes, references and money. Ink carries every action and row selection is a grey step; colour appears only in six semantic status tones, each always with a word.

nodes.label: Staff Playbooks
nodes.rationale: A searchable library of reviewed staff playbooks, tagged with English, Malay and Manglish search terms such as slip gaji, LO and surat tawaran, so guidance is reachable in the language the office actually uses.

nodes.label: Booking BK-9001 Lifecycle Flow
nodes.rationale: The worked eight-step flow from deposit and ingestion through banker chat, Jev extraction, human verification, Today queue activation, playbook guidance, live resolution and execution feeds the resolved case back into the stage conversion rates.

nodes.label: Where AI Helps And Where People Decide
nodes.rationale: AI accelerates clerical extraction and semantic retrieval but is never permitted to make operational or financial decisions; each domain names the human or deterministic governance that owns it.
nodes.norm_label: where ai helps and where people decide

nodes.label: TypeSafe Jev
nodes.rationale: A server-side classification and scoring engine: it accepts plain text and returns structured typed TypeScript objects with probabilities and confidence values, and never generates arbitrary text.

nodes.label: Jev 0.60 Confidence Threshold
nodes.rationale: Extractions at or above 0.60 confidence are offered as proposals staff confirm; below 0.60 the proposal is flagged Needs Review.

nodes.label: Jev Multi-Tier Fallback Ladder
nodes.rationale: Live call with a 3000ms timeout, then exact input-hash cache hit, then the latest cached answer for that booking marked stale, then neutral structural fallbacks marked unavailable, so the product works through demo presentations and network outages and staff can still record milestones by hand.

nodes.label: GET /api/snapshot Never Calls Jev Live
nodes.rationale: Page navigation must never wait on live AI processing. The snapshot does not walk the ladder at all: it re-checks each saved next_action and signals answer against the case's current state and marks it stale itself when the case has moved on.

nodes.label: Practitioner Survey (n = 8)
nodes.rationale: An anonymous survey run 18-22 September 2026 across sales and project marketing, project management, finance, construction, sales administration and legal conveyancing. 7 of 8 named loan rejection the single biggest cause of leakage and all 8 put it in their top three; half estimated only 0 to 2 of every 10 bookings reach a signed SPA.

nodes.label: Ranked Causes Of Booking Leakage
nodes.rationale: Loan rejection first (7 of 8), buyer withdrawal and incomplete documentation joint second (5 of 8), valuation shortfall third (3 of 8), slow bank processing last (1 of 8). Only 1 of 8 supported AI-estimating conversion risk, validating statistical forecasting over generative LLM prediction.

nodes.label: 30-Day Verified SPA Rate (North Star Metric)
nodes.rationale: Bookings signing a verified SPA within 30 days of booking divided by all eligible bookings in the cohort. It is a real commercial outcome readable inside one quarter, and enforcing a 30-day horizon halts inventory holding drag.

nodes.label: Quarterly Evaluation Window
nodes.rationale: A developer can enroll an intake cohort between day 15 and day 44 of a quarter, conclude all observation by day 74 and reconcile legal audits by day 84.

nodes.label: Illustrative Impact Calculation (40 x 20% uplift)
nodes.rationale: 40 eligible stalled bookings moving from 20% to 40% conversion gives 8 additional SPAs. These are planning assumptions to be replaced with pilot data, and a signed SPA is not cash: cash forecasting needs actual payment amounts and dates.

nodes.label: What Mortar Is Not (Functional Boundaries)
nodes.rationale: Not a CRM, not an autonomous decider, not a customer-facing chatbot, not a customer-facing portal, and not a privacy risk. It receives bookings after a deposit is paid, never unilaterally cancels or forfeits, and holds only synthetic data so no personal data is kept under the PDPA.

nodes.label: Prototype Versus Production Roadmap
nodes.rationale: The prototype exercises case mechanics on synthetic data; production moves to an ERP-calibrated engine, a PostgreSQL cluster with point-in-time recovery, SSO with RBAC, a VPC-hosted intelligence layer, bidirectional ERP integration, WhatsApp Cloud API webhooks and an OCR ingestion pipeline.

nodes.label: 12-Week Pilot Plan
nodes.rationale: Weeks 1-2 intake and baseline, 3-4 assisted queue, 5-8 live intervention cohort against a comparable control, 9-12 verification and evaluation, all designed to read the effect within one quarter.

nodes.label: Automated Action Preference Finding
nodes.rationale: Survey respondents named suggesting next actions by stage (4 of 8), checking documents for missing items (3 of 8) and summarising WhatsApp updates (3 of 8) as the safe areas for AI assistance.

nodes.label: Goals And Non-Goals
nodes.rationale: Three goals: close the visibility gap between deposit and SPA into a daily follow-up queue; introduce structured AI with no operational risk by reserving all state transitions for verified human confirmation; replace face-value booking projections with a stage-weighted 30-day forecast using Wilson intervals and Monte Carlo bounds.

nodes.label: Core Objective (Single Source Of Truth)
nodes.rationale: Give operational staff a single source of truth for booking progress so signings land inside the 30-day horizon rather than languishing off market.

nodes.label: Human In The Loop
nodes.rationale: Every AI suggestion remains a proposal until confirmed by an authorized staff member, preserving accountability across all departments.

nodes.label: Honest Accounting Rule
nodes.rationale: A booking is never counted as cash at face value, protecting financial planning from unrealized revenue.

nodes.label: Demo Script As Acceptance
nodes.rationale: The prototype is accepted when the deployed application executes a six-step pitch video script without error or manual intervention, ending in a Settings reset with a 30-second cooldown.

nodes.label: Secondary Operational Metrics
nodes.rationale: Stalled booking recovery, case dwell in unknown, forecast calibration by Brier score, AI extraction accuracy from unmodified confirmations, live Jev latency under 3 seconds, and fallback cache hit rate.

nodes.label: Three-Tier Architecture (SPA / Bun API / Neon Postgres)
nodes.rationale: One React 19 SPA, one Bun HTTP server on Cloud Run, and managed PostgreSQL on Neon, kept deliberately lean so a single container serves both static assets and the API, replacing a reverse proxy such as Nginx.
nodes.norm_label: three-tier architecture (spa / bun api / neon postgres)

nodes.label: Single HTTP Server (Bun.serve)
nodes.rationale: One Bun process serves frontend/dist with SPA routing fallbacks and handles all /api/* endpoints.

nodes.label: Neon PostgreSQL (Pooled Connections)
nodes.rationale: Neon holds relational state, connected through pooled connections via Bun's native SQL client; local development targets the Neon dev branch and production targets main.

nodes.label: @mortar/core (Pure TypeScript Library)
nodes.rationale: Pure TypeScript with an ES2020 target and zero DOM or Node dependencies: contract types, seeded PRNG simulation, event log derivation rules, financial risk formulas, forecasting math and fixture datasets. Browser and server both import it, so a booking has one definition and never two.

nodes.label: @mortar/jev (Server-Only TypeSafe Client)
nodes.rationale: Wraps the TypeSafe SDK to run probabilistic classifications server-side; the TypeSafe API key is restricted to the server process and never sent to the browser.

nodes.label: Ask Mortar Service (server/src/assistant/)
nodes.rationale: Grounded operational assistant over Google Gemini with five read-only snapshot tools, fenced untrusted message bodies, structured answers and booking citations, with zero write access.

nodes.label: PERSONA_PAGES And PersonaRoute Guard
nodes.rationale: Client-side route guarding redirects unauthorized routes to persona homes without masking data.

nodes.label: Unified Next Step Derivation (nextStep.ts)
nodes.rationale: Establishes a single rule-based move from ballInCourt as the default across cards and side sheets, surfacing Jev alternatives only when they differ.

nodes.label: SnapshotProvider (GET /api/snapshot)
nodes.rationale: The client loads the entire operational dataset lazily on the first useSnapshot() call, so public pages never hit the API; the provider retains the data, derives all views client-side with @mortar/core, sends mutations over REST and refreshes on completion.

nodes.label: Fixed Reference Date (REFERENCE_DATE = 2026-09-18)
nodes.rationale: Every view operates against a fixed 'Today'; live mutations stamp timestamps with simNow(referenceDate, clock), preserving wall-clock time in Malaysian time zone +08:00.

nodes.label: Caching Strategy (Cache-First Reads, Live-First Mutations)
nodes.rationale: Client page transitions never block on external model invocations.

nodes.label: Data Model And Schema
nodes.rationale: The PostgreSQL schema mirrors the TypeScript contract: snake_case columns against camelCase entities, so a booking has exactly one definition across both layers.

nodes.label: Table: meta (Key-Value Store)
nodes.rationale: Holds seed, referenceDate, resetAt and resetAtWall. resetAt is simulation time but resetAtWall is the real wall-clock timestamp, and it is what the 30-second reset cooldown reads, because simulation time's time-of-day wraps to 00:00 at midnight and cannot time a cooldown.

nodes.label: Table: bookings
nodes.rationale: Core booking records with project, unit, price, booking date, owner fields and a nested buyer JSONB holding contact details, financial metrics and property ownership counts.

nodes.label: Table: loan_applications
nodes.rationale: An application's status is never stored as an enum column; it is derived dynamically from confirmed events, so a case's bank state can never drift from its evidence.

nodes.label: Table: messages
nodes.rationale: Transcripts from buyers, bankers, solicitors or sales agents, with sender roles restricted to those four values.

nodes.label: Table: events (Auditable Event Log)
nodes.rationale: seq is drawn from the events_seq sequence and numbers rows in storage order; every ordered read sorts on occurred_at, seq, so two events recorded for the same instant keep the order they were entered in rather than an arbitrary one.

nodes.label: Event Ordering Rule (occurred_at, seq)
nodes.rationale: Two events recorded for the same instant (a same-day update stamped noon, say) must keep the order they were entered in, not an arbitrary one, so every ordered read of the event log sorts on occurred_at then seq.

nodes.label: Table: event_reviews (Append-Only Review Trail)
nodes.rationale: Carries no foreign key to events, so the review trail survives the event it reviewed and a reset from an older build can still truncate events without breaking event_reviews' own schema.

nodes.label: Table: jev_answers (Model Answer Cache)
nodes.rationale: Indexed on (kind, subject_id, created_at desc) to allow rapid cache resolution.

nodes.label: Table: imports (Undoable Import Batches)
nodes.rationale: The row itself is never deleted, so every removal leaves a trace; removed holds the undo's own snapshot of what it took out, with id, unit, project, buyer name and price but never the IC or phone, because the booking row is gone once the undo commits.

nodes.label: Event Model And Evidence Lifecycle
nodes.rationale: Events sit on three parallel tracks (sales, loan, legal) and carry an explicit verification state: confirmed advances the funnel, provisional is a Jev proposal awaiting review, disputed halts automatic progression and immediately triggers a stall reason, superseded stays in the ledger for auditability but does not influence case state.

nodes.label: Row-Locked Single Decision On A Proposal
nodes.rationale: Only a proposal still waiting may be reviewed; the server checks under a row lock and refuses a second decision with 409, and every successful review is appended to event_reviews so the gating rules apply to a reviewed proposal exactly as they do to a hand-recorded update.
nodes.norm_label: row-locked single decision on a proposal

nodes.label: API Reference (RESTful JSON)
nodes.rationale: Request and response bodies conform directly to contract types, and validation uses explicit type guards with no third-party schema validation library loaded.

nodes.label: Forecast And Backtest Method
nodes.rationale: The engine replaces uncalibrated face-value booking sums with stage-weighted statistical probabilities over a 30-calendar-day horizon from the initial booking deposit.

nodes.label: Statistical Forecast (Stratified Stage Rates)
nodes.rationale: Rates are grouped by stage and age cohort (0-9, 10-19, 20-29 days); if an age cohort has fewer than 8 resolved cases the calculation falls back to the aggregate stage rate and then to the global baseline rate.

nodes.label: Wilson 95% Score Interval
nodes.rationale: Brown, Cai and DasGupta (2001) recommend Wilson or Jeffreys intervals for samples of 40 or fewer, where the textbook Wald interval is unreliable; every stage conversion rate is bounded this way to reflect small-sample uncertainty.

nodes.label: Monte Carlo Aggregate Distribution (2000 Draws)
nodes.rationale: Expected signings equal the arithmetic sum of individual booking probabilities; the high and low bands are the 10th and 90th percentiles of 2000 seeded random outcome draws.

nodes.label: Backtest Validation (Brier Score, Calibration Table)
nodes.rationale: The log is split at REFERENCE_DATE minus 30 days (2026-08-19); probabilities are calibrated only from events before the cutoff and scored against the observed outcomes in the following 30-day window from the full log.

nodes.label: Backtest Caption (Proves The Method, Not The Business)
nodes.rationale: Per the documentation guidelines, the backtest card states plainly that a backtest on simulated data proves the method, not the business.
nodes.norm_label: backtest caption (proves the method, not the business)

nodes.label: DEFAULT_ASSUMPTIONS (Labelled, Tagged, Sourced)
nodes.rationale: Every rate and threshold the simulation uses lives in DEFAULT_ASSUMPTIONS with a label, unit, tag and source matching the seed table in the front-end simulation study. Untagged numbers are assumptions.

nodes.label: Financing-Risk Method (financingRisk)
nodes.rationale: Calculates an advisory credit flag for each buyer as an early warning for sales administration rather than a blocking gate on bookings.

nodes.label: Debt Service Ratio Formula
nodes.rationale: DSR = (monthly commitments + monthly instalment) / gross monthly income, where the instalment is an annuity on price x margin at 4.2% over min(35, 70 - age) years.

nodes.label: Risk Categorization (DSR 40% / 35% Thresholds)
nodes.rationale: DSR above 40% is high risk; 35-40% or a missing income document is medium; under 35% with complete documents is low.

nodes.label: Jev Integration (jev-latest)
nodes.rationale: Jev is a probabilistic reasoning engine: it reads text only and emits typed answers with confidence scores and probability distributions. It never generates text.

nodes.label: Jev Fan-Out Pattern
nodes.rationale: Every intelligence task dispatches multiple typed questions (Choice, Score, Noul) across a single state payload, so one API call yields event, document, owner, urgency and fit together.

nodes.label: Jev Job: signals
nodes.rationale: Responsiveness and hesitation are scored from buyer messages with timestamps and response gaps computed in code, so the timing evidence is deterministic rather than model-estimated.

nodes.label: Jev Question Design Rules
nodes.rationale: TypeSafe Jev does not transmit question IDs to the model, so every question prompt contains its complete semantic definition and criteria; every Choice question carries an explicit no-match option (no_update, none, wait) to prevent forced misclassification; below 0.60 confidence the UI renders a visible Needs Review tag.

nodes.label: Input Hash (SHA-256 Of Canonical JSON)
nodes.rationale: Computed as the SHA-256 digest of stable canonical JSON representing { kind, state, questionVersion } so an exact cache hit is provably the same question about the same state.

nodes.label: Precompute Fixtures (bun run jev:precompute)
nodes.rationale: Build verification calls Jev live once per fixture message, signals/next action/default-query playbooks per story booking and next actions for up to 25 stalled generated bookings, writing server/fixtures/jev-cache.json. This keeps demo executions under 120 calls and avoids live latency during presentations.

nodes.label: Two Sources Of stale: true
nodes.rationale: The ladder's Subject Stale Fallback marks an answer stale when the exact input hash is missing and the latest answer for the subject is served instead. GET /api/snapshot marks next_action and signals stale a second, separate way: it always serves the latest saved answer, then flags it stale if the case has changed since. Both reach the frontend as the same JevMeta.stale flag.

nodes.label: Synthetic Data Guarantee
nodes.rationale: No real customer names, NRIC numbers, telephone numbers or financial statements are ingested. Identity numbers use reserved formatting 000000-00-XXXX and phone numbers the fictional prefix +60 00-000 XXXX. The /import route is kept clear of live data during public demonstrations.

nodes.label: Secret Management
nodes.rationale: Credentials live in a git-ignored .env; TEST_DATABASE_URL is dedicated to the isolated Neon test database and is never pointed at production; no VITE_* variable exposes a token to the browser; Cloud Run receives keys as secure environment variables populated from GitHub Secrets.

nodes.label: Gemini Free-Tier Caveat
nodes.rationale: On the free tier Google may use prompts and responses to improve products, so Ask Mortar must only process simulated data; real buyer data requires a paid tier or Vertex AI under a Data Processing Agreement.

nodes.label: PDPA 2024 Compliance
nodes.rationale: Synthetic records describe no identifiable person so the prototype holds no personal data, but the platform is architected for future onboarding: the event log preserves who reported and verified every mutation as groundwork for 72-hour breach notification, PDPC May 2026 automated-decision guidelines apply once the forecast scores real buyers, and every persona sees the same figures so persona sets workflow defaults, not data access.

nodes.label: Data Retention (7 Years / 24-Month Disposal)
nodes.rationale: Companies Act 2016 s245(3) and Income Tax Act 1967 s82(1)(a) each set seven years and pull toward keeping; the PDPA 2010 and the PDPS 2015 Retention Standard pull the other way, keeping personal data only as long as its purpose lasts and preparing a disposal schedule for inactive data on a 24-month period. AMLA 2001 s17 sets six years for reporting institutions but names estate agency practice, not developers. Today nothing is deleted in normal use, event_reviews outlive the events they reviewed, undo import keeps a removed snapshot without IC or phone, a real-data deployment must set MORTAR_DEMO_RESET off, and a 7-year guarantee needs regular database exports kept outside the app.

nodes.label: Containerization (Multi-Stage oven/bun:1.3.14-slim)
nodes.rationale: The container packages static client assets directly alongside the API runtime, so one instance serves both web traffic and backend queries.

nodes.label: Deployment Workflow (Keyless Workload Identity Federation)
nodes.rationale: Authenticates to Google Cloud with Workload Identity Federation, so no service account keys are stored in GitHub, then builds into Artifact Registry, rolls out to Cloud Run in asia-southeast1 and injects DATABASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY and GEMINI_API_KEY from repository secrets.

nodes.label: CI Gates (bun run check / format / test)
nodes.rationale: Every proposed change must pass ESLint, TypeScript workspace typechecking and the Vitest suites; CI passes the TEST_DATABASE_URL secret so the database suite actually runs.
nodes.norm_label: ci gates (bun run check / format / test)

nodes.label: Design: Mortar
nodes.rationale: The design research is turned into binding values: exact tokens for typeface, colour, layout, motion and every component. Where this document and a research page disagree, this one wins.

nodes.label: Mortar Design System In Figma
nodes.rationale: The public Figma file and this document use the same token and style names, so a design and its build compare line by line.

nodes.label: Seven Binding Design Decisions

nodes.label: Plain Language Rule
nodes.rationale: Mortar is read by sales, loan and legal staff, not engineers. Industry terms stay (SPA, LO, RM, panel bank, disbursement, solicitor) and Jev stays because staff refer to it by name; software, statistics and data-pipeline vocabulary never reaches the screen. Name the thing, not the mechanism; say when, not what state; Jev acts, it does not report status; errors say what to do; no abbreviations we invented.

nodes.rationale: Select, date picker, menu, tooltip, file drop, checkbox and scrollbar are Mortar components built on Radix/shadcn and restyled. No alert, confirm or prompt.

nodes.label: Acceptance: Fourteen Criteria
nodes.rationale: A screen or component ships when all fourteen criteria hold across both light and dark modes: no raw hex outside globals.css, zero native controls, explicit status wording, WCAG AA 4.5:1 contrast with a 2px focus ring, tabular numerals, a single Primary action per view, verified at 1280/1440px and usable to 1024px, dual-mode inspection, a scrolling landing that leads with a viewport, footer scope, bare sign-in, Title Case, clean card edges, and plain language.

nodes.label: Single Primary Action Rule
nodes.rationale: A view offers one Primary action, not one Primary button. Where a list repeats that action per row, every item renders it Primary; what never appears is a second different Primary action on the same view, or a list that fills the first item and leaves the rest outlined.

nodes.label: Clean Card Edges
nodes.rationale: Every card, stat tile and panel sits on the white page ground carrying --shadow-card and a --card-border hairline, and nothing else. No coloured strip, bar, rule or accent runs along any edge, and no grey band sits behind a card to separate it from the page.

nodes.label: Do Not List
nodes.rationale: The consolidated list of prohibitions: no glass, blur, gradients or glow blobs in the app; no coloured edge strips; no software or statistics vocabulary in visible strings; no grey band behind cards; no chromatic accent beyond the six status tones and never red except severe risk and irreversible destructive actions; no call to action in the landing header; no video or autoplay; no row washes or zebra striping; no emoji icons or a second icon set; no third typeface; no window.alert/confirm/prompt; no native select, date or file inputs; never more than one Primary button; no 999px pill radii; no footer outside / and /faq.

nodes.label: The One Rule That Governs Everything
nodes.rationale: A booking is never counted as cash at face value. Every booking enters the forecast at the historical conversion rate of its current stage, enforced in @mortar/core rather than in a dashboard label somebody could forget. So the forecast can only move toward honesty, success is one number readable within a quarter, and every booking is screened within 48 hours instead of blocking bookings upstream.

nodes.label: Gotcha: Both Halves Of /forecast Read One Log
nodes.rationale: forecast() projects forward and leakage() counts backward, both from the same confirmed events in @mortar/core, so what signed and what died cannot drift apart. nodes.label: Gotcha: open Is Not live
nodes.rationale: deriveCase computes both. live adds ageDays < HORIZON_DAYS (30) and is what the forecast counts; open is just unsigned and not exited. Stall reasons derive from open, because gating them on live hid every case that had sat longest, the ones most worth chasing. Anything reading stallReasons must filter on open, and brain.test.ts pins Ask's stalled set to Today's so the two cannot drift apart again.

nodes.label: Gotcha: Persona Pages Drive The Sidebar And Route Guard

nodes.label: Gotcha: No Data Masking
nodes.rationale: PERSONA_PERMISSIONS is gone. Nothing in Mortar partitions or hides data per persona; every persona sees identical figures. Persona sets defaults such as preset filters and home views, not data access.

nodes.label: Gotcha: One Next Step Per Case (nextStep.ts)
nodes.rationale: The rule-based move from ballInCourt is the default everywhere (Today, Bookings table, CaseQuickView). nodes.label: Karpathy Guidelines Tradeoff
nodes.rationale: These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

nodes.label: Rule: Think Before Coding
nodes.rationale: Don't assume, don't hide confusion, surface tradeoffs: state assumptions explicitly, present multiple interpretations rather than picking silently, say when a simpler approach exists, and stop and name what is confusing rather than guessing.

nodes.label: Rule: Simplicity First
nodes.rationale: Minimum code that solves the problem, nothing speculative: no features beyond what was asked, no abstractions for single-use code, no unrequested flexibility, no error handling for impossible scenarios. If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

nodes.label: Rule: Surgical Changes
nodes.rationale: Touch only what you must: do not improve adjacent code, refactor things that are not broken, or match existing style differently. Remove orphans your own changes created; mention unrelated dead code rather than deleting it. Every changed line should trace directly to the request.

nodes.label: Rule: Goal-Driven Execution
nodes.rationale: Transform tasks into verifiable goals: add validation becomes write tests for invalid inputs then make them pass. Strong success criteria let a loop run independently; weak ones require constant clarification.

nodes.label: Problem Overview (Quoted Brief)
nodes.rationale: A property project launches, Sales books units and the launch is reported as a success, but a meaningful share of those bookings never converts to a signed SPA.

nodes.label: Your Mission (Seven Deliverables)
nodes.rationale: Rank the causes, find where bookings stall, propose at least one practical measurable change, show the derivation, join up Sales, Credit/Loan Admin and Legal, place AI honestly, and build something a Sales Administration Executive could actually use day to day.

nodes.label: Tension (The Sales View And The Finance View)
nodes.rationale: Sales does not control bank credit and fears stricter pre-qualification will reduce bookings and affect launch momentum; Finance views a non-converting booking as not a sale while it still consumes inventory and cost, so forecasting cash on bookings forecasts from a number known to be unreliable. The challenge is not to make one team the problem.
nodes.norm_label: tension (the sales view and the finance view)

nodes.label: Constraints (12 Weeks, No New CRM, No Authority)
nodes.rationale: 12 weeks, no new CRM, no consultant, no vendor; no authority over the sales director, panel bankers or panel solicitors, two of whom do not work for the developer at all; whatever exists at the end of the first fortnight, you built yourself.
nodes.norm_label: constraints (12 weeks, no new crm, no authority)

nodes.label: How Do You Know It Worked? (One Number)
nodes.rationale: Success is measured through one number readable within one quarter, and it must represent a real business outcome, behaviour or cash movement, not a dashboard or a report someone has to open.
nodes.norm_label: how do you know it worked? (one number)

nodes.label: The Challenge In Plain Terms
nodes.rationale: A booking is a promise to buy, not a sale, yet the developer forecasts cash as if it were one; the real sale is the signed SPA, often weeks later, and nobody watches the whole gap between the two.

nodes.label: Why The Obvious Fix Fails
nodes.rationale: Screening buyers harder before booking looks like the answer and most surveyed practitioners want an early financing check, but Sales resists any gate that slows a launch and the brief rules out making one team the problem. The answer must manage bookings better after they happen, not block them.

nodes.label: How Mortar Answers The Brief (Not A Screening Tool)
nodes.rationale: A prediction alone changes nothing. Mortar accepts every booking, watches it until it signs or fails, and prompts action when it starts to slip; knowing a booking is at risk leads to save it, release it, or count it honestly. The only screening is an advisory financing-risk chip that says watch this one closely, never reject.

nodes.label: A Company Brain For Booking-To-SPA Conversion
nodes.rationale: Research and platform concept for Chin Hin Group, Malaysia, researched 19 September 2026. A researched proposal, not a tested deployment: no Chin Hin internal records were available, so the company's systems, access rights, leakage rates and leading causes remain to be established.
nodes.norm_label: a company brain for booking-to-spa conversion

nodes.label: Recommendation (Case Record, Staff Knowledge, Owned Actions)
nodes.rationale: Build a shared booking workspace with three connected capabilities: a reliable case record, searchable staff knowledge, and follow-up actions with owners. A company brain can supply the knowledge capability, but the business benefit comes when that knowledge changes what happens to a live booking. Start with one project and one Sales Administration Executive; a company-wide rollout and a sophisticated knowledge graph can follow evidence that the small version helps bookings convert.
nodes.norm_label: recommendation (case record, staff knowledge, owned actions)

nodes.label: Five Layers Of Information
nodes.rationale: Current case facts (structured records, dated evidence, a responsible verifier), staff experience (searchable case examples and reviewed guidance), formal requirements (versioned source, owner and review date), work in progress (task, owner, due date, completion evidence) and estimates (a measured method, stated horizon and uncertainty) have different reliability requirements and different handling.

nodes.label: The Four Practical Questions
nodes.rationale: What is happening with this booking and what evidence supports that answer; what is blocking progress and what information is missing; what should the responsible person do next using relevant experience; did that action lead to an executed SPA or another verified outcome.

nodes.label: What Central Means Here
nodes.rationale: Central means a consistent place to find permitted information. Sales may need to know income documents are incomplete without seeing the buyer's full bank statements, and some records can remain in their original systems with links and permission-controlled summaries in the workspace.

nodes.label: Open-Source Projects Worth Learning From
nodes.rationale: Alternatives to evaluate, not a list to install together; each is scoped with its licence and boundary.

nodes.label: GBrain (MIT)
nodes.rationale: Persistent agent memory with sources, retrieval and knowledge relationships. A useful foundation for preserving approved experience, but the booking model, department workflow and business verification still need building, and a shared company brain needs Postgres or Supabase, an HTTPS MCP server and OAuth clients. Its company-brain tutorial is the recommended starting point, and read access is source-level: folders inside a shared source are not independent confidentiality boundaries.

nodes.label: Onyx (MIT outside ee/)
nodes.rationale: A user-facing AI platform with chat, document retrieval and connectors; a strong candidate when the first need is staff searching internal knowledge through a ready-made interface. Enterprise features sit under a separate licence, so verify which permission and administration features the chosen edition supplies.

nodes.label: RAGFlow (Apache-2.0)
nodes.rationale: Document ingestion and retrieval including scanned material with citations; worth evaluating if retrieving information from PDFs and scans is the main difficulty. Its self-hosting baseline includes at least 16 GB RAM.

nodes.label: Cognee (Apache-2.0)
nodes.rationale: An agent-memory platform organizing information into a searchable knowledge graph; a candidate for a custom application whose assistants need persistent, connected knowledge. Budget for application development, source mapping and access-control integration.

nodes.label: Graphiti (Apache-2.0)
nodes.rationale: A framework for incrementally building knowledge graphs that represent changing relationships and facts over time; particularly relevant if knowing what was true at a particular time becomes essential. A developer component needing Neo4j or FalkorDB, distinct from Zep's managed service.

nodes.label: Khoj (AGPL-3.0)
nodes.rationale: A self-hostable second-brain assistant with document search, custom agents and automations. Check licence obligations; development has slowed and the latest release is a March 2026 beta.

nodes.label: Docling (MIT code)
nodes.rationale: Converts documents into structured content including OCR for scanned material; a document-processing component rather than a company brain, for a custom ingestion pipeline.

nodes.label: Dify (source-available, modified Apache)
nodes.rationale: A visual environment for building AI workflows, retrieval applications and tool integrations, but its licence restricts multi-tenant operation and frontend branding, so it should not be grouped unqualified with standard permissive open-source projects.

nodes.label: How I Would Narrow The Choice
nodes.rationale: Choose by the bottleneck: knowledge hard to find, evaluate Onyx; scans hard to read and search, evaluate RAGFlow or Docling in a custom app; building your own assistant and interface, GBrain or Cognee; changing relationships hard to reconstruct, Graphiti after the basic case records work; actions forgotten despite adequate information, begin with a shared task queue and clear ownership because a new memory engine may add little. Starting choice: a small structured case application plus searchable, approved playbooks, adding a knowledge backend only after trying the same small set of real, anonymized questions against it. Do not make the pilot depend on deploying several AI platforms.

nodes.rationale: Each booking has one shared case page backed by a history of events; the home screen is a work queue of cases needing an action, evidence or a decision today, and department-specific views show the same underlying cases.

nodes.label: Does A Knowledge Graph Help?
nodes.rationale: Potentially: a graph represents entities and relationships with retained sources and dates, and becomes useful when recurring questions involve several connections. But a relational database with linked tables and an event history can already answer many of these questions; for a small pilot begin there, and add a graph when specific questions are genuinely cumbersome or unreliable to answer, comparing it against that baseline. Neither Microsoft GraphRAG nor Graphiti independently establishes the true cause of leakage or calculates a trustworthy conversion probability; the most valuable first capability is reliable evidence and follow-up ownership, with the graph an optional implementation choice behind that experience.

nodes.label: Microsoft GraphRAG (Maintenance Mode)
nodes.rationale: Extracts relationships and community summaries from documents to support retrieval, including broad questions across a collection; the project is now largely in maintenance mode, taking bug and security fixes but no new features.

nodes.label: Where AI Helps, And Where People Decide
nodes.rationale: Avoid an autonomous agent that changes official status, promises approval, releases inventory or learns operational policy from every conversation without review; one assistant with constrained functions is sufficient initially, and separate agents for every department are optional. Apply access controls before retrieval and to attachments, generated summaries and saved answers. Documents and messages are evidence, not instructions that can authorize an agent to act.

nodes.label: Scope (Front-End Only)
nodes.rationale: No server, no database, no live AI calls and no real buyer data; everything runs in the React app and @mortar/core, matching the browser-only architecture in the project README.

nodes.label: Roadmap, Not Prototype
nodes.rationale: Deferred: any company-brain engine, live AI extraction of messages and documents, search by meaning across languages, OCR of scanned documents, modelling banker and solicitor capacity as queues, and calibrating the rates on real consented company data.

nodes.label: Why The Company-Brain Tools Wait
nodes.rationale: All nine projects exist and carry the stated licences, but none can run inside a static single-page app: each needs a server process, a database or search engine, and usually an LLM or embedding key that must stay server-side. A live Gemini call has the same problem: Google's guidance is never to expose an API key client-side, and a static bundle has nowhere to hide one.

nodes.label: Stages (Funnel Plus Exits)
nodes.rationale: Booking, loan application, Letter of Offer, SPA signed, loan agreement and disbursement, plus cancelled and lapsed as exits; conversion means reaching SPA signed, with separate overlapping loan and legal tracks, one to three bank applications per booking so one rejection does not fail the booking, and unknown shown rather than progressing or failed when there is no recent evidence.

nodes.label: Generator (Stage-Transition Monte Carlo)
nodes.rationale: A stage-transition Monte Carlo drawing the next outcome and a dwell time at every stage. Full discrete-event simulation only pays off when modelling shared capacity such as a banker's queue, which is roadmap. The generator is seeded (sfc32 or mulberry32) so the same seed gives the same data, and SimJS and seedrandom are skipped. @faker-js/faker is skipped: no Malaysian locale and over 5 MiB minified, so short hand-written lists of Malay, Chinese and Indian names, a fictional project, fictional panel banks and fictional law firms are used instead. About 150 bookings against a fixed reference date so screenshots match the pitch video, and every screen including 'as of' views derives from one event log.

nodes.label: Forecast And Backtest Rules
nodes.rationale: A 30-day horizon from booking; stage rate counts bookings that signed within the horizon divided by resolved bookings that reached the stage, counting only cases resolved before the forecast date. Small samples get a Wilson or Jeffreys interval because the Wald interval is unreliable at 40 or fewer. Expected signings are the sum of each live booking's probability, with a range from repeated random draws. Backtesting cuts the log at a past date and estimates rates only from what was known then. The caveat is stated on screen: a backtest on data the simulator produced proves the code works, not that the business behaves this way.

nodes.label: Messages And Proposed Updates
nodes.rationale: 20 to 40 WhatsApp-style messages in English, Malay, Chinese and Manglish with the extracted update already attached, committed as JSON. The case page shows each extraction as proposed and staff confirm, dispute or dismiss it, so the demo runs no model. If an LLM writes the fixtures it is prompted with invented details only, because Gemini's free tier may use submitted content to improve Google products and human reviewers may read it.

nodes.label: Merging Into main Deploys To The Live Site
nodes.rationale: There is no staging step between merging into main and the live site, so a pull request is the last chance to catch a mistake. Everything else in the guide exists to protect that moment.
nodes.norm_label: merging into main deploys to the live site

nodes.label: The Journey Of A Change
nodes.rationale: Issue -> Branch -> Commits -> Pull Request -> Review -> Squash Merge -> Live. Each step answers what and why, keeps the branch your own copy, commits in small steps, lets CI check it, needs a teammate approval, lands one commit on main, and confirms the change on the live site.

nodes.label: Start With An Issue
nodes.rationale: Every change except a typo fix starts as an issue, so the team agrees on the what and why before anyone writes code.

nodes.label: Use A Form, Blank Issues Are Off
nodes.rationale: Pick Bug Report or Feature Or Change so every issue carries the fields the team needs to act on it.
nodes.norm_label: use a form, blank issues are off

nodes.label: One Problem Per Issue
nodes.rationale: If you find a second problem, open a second issue, so each issue stays small enough to review and close.

nodes.label: Check For Duplicates And Conflicts Before Opening An Issue
nodes.rationale: Search open and closed issues and pull requests with gh first. Comment on a duplicate instead of opening another, and link any issue that overlaps or conflicts. See docs/agents/github.md.
nodes.norm_label: check for duplicates and conflicts before opening an issue

nodes.label: Branch Naming Convention <type>/<short-topic>
nodes.rationale: Lowercase with hyphens, prefixed by one of five types: feat (new capability), fix (something broken), ui (look and layout only, no behaviour change), docs (documents only), chore (tooling, dependencies, config, cleanup). Example: feat/chase-quick-confirm.

nodes.label: Start From Fresh main
nodes.rationale: Run git switch main and git pull before branching, so the branch carries no stale history and the pull request merges cleanly.

nodes.label: One Branch, One Change
nodes.rationale: Do not reuse a merged branch for new work, so review and revert stay scoped to one change.

nodes.label: Stay Up To Date Before Review
nodes.rationale: If GitHub shows Update branch on the pull request, click it before asking for review, so the reviewer sees the code as it will merge.
nodes.norm_label: stay up to date before review

nodes.label: Commit Message Format type(scope): what changed
nodes.rationale: Lowercase and imperative, like an instruction. Type is the same list as branch types; scope is optional and names the area touched, such as chase, import, legal, forecast, landing or survey.
nodes.norm_label: commit message format type(scope): what changed

nodes.label: Small Steps, One Working Step Per Commit
nodes.rationale: Commit each working step separately, not a whole day in one commit, so a reviewer can follow the change and any single commit can be reverted.
nodes.norm_label: small steps, one working step per commit

nodes.label: Pre-Commit Hook Formats Staged Files
nodes.rationale: The hook formats staged files automatically; if it fails, read the message, fix it and commit again rather than skipping it.

nodes.label: One Thing Per Pull Request
nodes.rationale: If the title needs the word and, split it. Aim for under about 400 changed lines, not counting bun.lock, so review and revert stay tractable.

nodes.label: Fill In The Pull Request Template
nodes.rationale: Every section, in plain words, so a reviewer can judge the change without asking. Link the issue with Closes #123 so it closes on merge.
nodes.norm_label: fill in the pull request template

nodes.label: Run The Checks Locally Before Pushing
nodes.rationale: Run bun run check, then bun run format. CI runs the same checks and blocks the merge if they fail, so running them locally only saves a round trip.
nodes.norm_label: run the checks locally before pushing

nodes.label: Check Open Pull Requests For Overlap
nodes.rationale: Compare the files you touch with every open pull request (gh pr view <number> --json files) and name any overlap in the description, so two people do not silently fight over the same lines.
nodes.norm_label: check open pull requests for overlap

nodes.label: Refresh The Graphify Graph Last
nodes.rationale: Make graphify update . the last commit so main always carries a current graph. See docs/agents/graphify.md.

nodes.label: Show UI Changes With Screenshots
nodes.rationale: Attach before and after screenshots for anything visible, since a reviewer cannot see the rendered result from a diff.

nodes.label: Follow The Design Guide And Shared UI Components
nodes.rationale: UI must follow docs/DESIGN.md and use the components in frontend/src/components/ui/, never browser-native inputs, selects or date pickers, so Mortar stays visually consistent and accessible.
nodes.norm_label: follow the design guide and shared ui components

nodes.label: Update The Docs In The Same Pull Request
nodes.rationale: If behaviour changed, update the PRD, TRD or docs/agents/notes.md in the same pull request, so the docs never drift from the deployed behaviour.
nodes.norm_label: update the docs in the same pull request

nodes.label: Draft While Unfinished
nodes.rationale: Open the pull request as a Draft until it is ready for review, so early feedback is invited without pulling a half-finished change into review.

nodes.label: Never Merge Your Own Pull Request
nodes.rationale: Wait for one teammate's approval, because a pull request is the last chance to catch a mistake before the live site.
nodes.norm_label: never merge your own pull request

nodes.label: Green Checks Only
nodes.rationale: Merge only when every check shows a green tick, since merging ships straight to the live site.

nodes.label: Answer Every Comment Then Resolve The Thread
nodes.rationale: Reply or push a fix, then resolve the thread, so no reviewer concern is left silently open at merge time.
nodes.norm_label: answer every comment then resolve the thread

nodes.label: Squash And Merge
nodes.rationale: Always choose Squash and merge so main gets one clean commit per change, and edit the squash title into the commit format, which keeps main readable as the change history.

nodes.label: Delete The Branch After Merging
nodes.rationale: Click Delete branch after merging, so the branch list shows only live work and no one branches off an already-merged copy.

nodes.label: Check The Live Site After The Deploy
nodes.rationale: Open the live site after the deploy finishes and try the change as a real user would, since green CI does not prove the change works in the deployed bundle.
nodes.norm_label: check the live site after the deploy

nodes.label: Never Do These
nodes.rationale: The hard prohibitions: push straight to main, commit secrets, commit real buyer data, force-push a shared branch, and bypass the checks.

nodes.label: No Pushes Straight To main
nodes.rationale: Always go through a pull request, because the pull request is the last review before the live site.

nodes.label: Never Commit Secrets
nodes.rationale: No .env files, API keys, passwords or tokens. Use .env.example for placeholders only, so a placeholder can never be mistaken for a live credential.

nodes.label: Never Commit Real Buyer Data
nodes.rationale: No real names, IC numbers, phone numbers or bank details in code, test data, screenshots or issues; all Mortar data is synthetic. See docs/TRD.md#data-retention.

nodes.label: Never Force-Push A Shared Branch
nodes.rationale: Never run git push --force on a branch someone else works on, because it silently destroys their commits.

nodes.label: Never Bypass The Checks
nodes.rationale: Do not disable a test, lint rule or hook to make a failure go away; ask for help instead, because a disabled check is invisible protection that never runs again.

nodes.label: When Something Breaks On The Live Site
nodes.rationale: Three steps: tell the team first in chat with a screenshot and page link; revert rather than patch, by clicking Revert on the merged pull request and merging the revert pull request, which restores the last working version within minutes; then fix calmly through a bug issue and a new branch on the normal journey.
nodes.norm_label: when something breaks on the live site

nodes.label: Working With AI Coding Agents
nodes.rationale: AI agents are welcome, but the human owns everything they write.

nodes.label: Read The Diff Before Committing
nodes.rationale: Read every changed line before committing. If you cannot explain a change, do not ship it, because unexplained code becomes unreviewable and unmaintainable code.

nodes.label: Keep AI Agents On Task
nodes.rationale: Ask for one change at a time, matching one issue; large mixed changes from an agent are the fastest way to a messy repo.

nodes.label: Graph First, Then Grep
nodes.rationale: Have agents query the Graphify graph (graphify query) before grepping; it answers most questions for far fewer tokens.

nodes.label: Point Agents At The Rules
nodes.rationale: Agents read AGENTS.md, which links back to this guide, so the written rules reach the agent instead of living only in a human's head.

nodes.label: Reviews And Merging
nodes.rationale: The gate between a finished pull request and the live site: one teammate's approval, green checks, every comment answered, squash and merge, branch deleted, live site checked.

nodes.label: Bug Report Issue Form
nodes.rationale: For when something in Mortar is broken or behaves wrongly. Titled with the Bug: prefix and labelled bug.

nodes.label: Describe What You Saw, Not What You Think The Cause Is
nodes.rationale: Opening note: Thanks for reporting. Plain words are fine. The reporter's guess about the cause is treated as unreliable, so the report is asked for as observation rather than diagnosis.
nodes.norm_label: describe what you saw, not what you think the cause is

nodes.label: What Happened
nodes.rationale: Required textarea: what went wrong, including any error message word for word, so the developer can search logs for the exact text.

nodes.label: What You Expected
nodes.rationale: Required textarea: what should have happened instead, which separates a genuine defect from intended behaviour.

nodes.label: Steps To Reproduce
nodes.rationale: Required textarea asking for the exact steps someone else can follow, with a worked example placeholder (sign in as Sales Admin, open Today, click the first card, see the error) because a bug another person can reproduce is a bug that can be verified and regression-tested.

nodes.label: Where: Live Site / Running Locally / Both
nodes.rationale: Required dropdown separating deployed-only faults from local-only faults, which points straight at whether the deploy or the dev environment is at fault.
nodes.norm_label: where: live site / running locally / both

nodes.label: Area
nodes.rationale: Required dropdown of Mortar's surfaces: Sales Admin (Today), Loan Admin (Bookings), Legal Admin (Legal), Case page, Forecast, Add Bookings, Settings, Ask Mortar, Several pages, Landing or sign-in, Not sure. The persona-shaped options route the bug to the persona who owns it.

nodes.label: Screenshots Or Recording
nodes.rationale: Optional field for dragging in images or a short video, because a visual fault is hard to convey in words.

nodes.label: Data Check
nodes.rationale: A required checkbox the reporter must tick confirming the report and screenshots contain no real buyer names, IC numbers, phone numbers or bank details. Because screenshots are encouraged, the form pushes the privacy rule to the exact moment a real name could be pasted or photographed into the issue.

nodes.label: Duplicate And Conflict Check
nodes.rationale: A required checkbox the reporter must tick, backed by a prompt to search first with gh issue list --state all --search "<keywords>" and gh pr list --state all --search "<keywords>". It turns the duplicate-search rule from advice into a form field that cannot be skipped, and gives the exact commands rather than the principle.

nodes.label: Blank Issues Disabled
nodes.rationale: blank_issues_enabled: false, so every issue arrives with the fields a form defines rather than as a free-form note.

nodes.label: Contact Link: How We Ship Changes
nodes.rationale: Because blank issues are off, the chooser shows a single link to .github/CONTRIBUTING.md on main with the text Read this before opening your first issue or pull request, so a person who wants to file something unprompted still lands on the rules first.
nodes.norm_label: contact link: how we ship changes

nodes.label: Feature Or Change Issue Form
nodes.rationale: For suggesting something new, or a change to how Mortar works, looks or reads. Titled with the Feature: prefix and labelled enhancement.

nodes.label: Start From The Problem, Not The Solution
nodes.rationale: Opening note: A clear problem makes a better change. Asking for the problem first leaves room for a solution different from the one the reporter had in mind.
nodes.norm_label: start from the problem, not the solution

nodes.label: The Problem
nodes.rationale: Required textarea: what is hard, slow, confusing or missing today, and for whom, with a placeholder naming a persona (Sales Admin has to open every case to see why it is stuck), because naming the affected persona is what makes the request actionable.

nodes.label: The Change
nodes.rationale: Required textarea: what should happen instead, with sketches and screenshots welcome, so the shape of the change can be shown rather than only described.

nodes.label: Done When
nodes.rationale: Required textarea asking for a short checklist that proves the change works, with a placeholder of checkbox lines phrased as observable outcomes (each Today card shows the stall reason in one sentence; the card has one button for the next action), so acceptance is agreed before the code is written.

nodes.label: Area
nodes.rationale: Required dropdown of the same persona-shaped surfaces as the bug form, plus Docs or research and Tooling or repo, so non-product work is filed in the same tracker and sorted by area.

nodes.label: Pitch Priority
nodes.rationale: Required dropdown asking how much the request matters for the Chin Hin pitch, with options Blocks the pitch, Improves the pitch, After the pitch. It ties ordering to an external deadline rather than to whoever filed first.

nodes.label: Duplicate And Conflict Check
nodes.rationale: The same required checkbox and gh search prompt as the bug form: search open and closed issues and pull requests and link any that overlap or conflict. Duplicated deliberately so the rule holds whichever form someone reaches for.

nodes.label: Pull Request Template
nodes.rationale: Carries the title format, the deploy warning and a pointer to .github/CONTRIBUTING.md in a hidden HTML comment, so the rules are visible to the author without cluttering the rendered description.

nodes.label: What Changed
nodes.rationale: One to three sentences in plain words about what someone will notice, aimed at the reader of the changelog rather than the reader of the diff.

nodes.label: Why
nodes.rationale: The rationale for the change, prefilled with Closes # so the linked issue closes automatically on merge.

nodes.label: Type Of Change
nodes.rationale: Checkbox list mirroring the branch and commit types: Feature (a new capability), Fix (something was broken), UI (look and layout only), Docs (documents only), Chore (tooling, dependencies or config).

nodes.label: How To Check It
nodes.rationale: Numbered steps a reviewer can follow, with a worked example (sign in as Sales Admin, open Today, click the first card), so verification is written down next to the change and can be repeated on the live site after the deploy.

nodes.label: Screenshots
nodes.rationale: A before/after table for anything visible, to be deleted if nothing is, which keeps visual work reviewable while not forcing an empty table on backend changes.

nodes.label: Checklist
nodes.rationale: The closing self-check: one thing and no and in the title; bun run check and bun run format run and CI green; open pull requests checked for overlapping files and related issues linked; the last commit refreshes the Graphify graph; the whole diff read including anything an AI agent wrote; UI follows docs/DESIGN.md with no browser-native inputs or selects; docs updated if behaviour changed; no secrets, .env files or real buyer data.

nodes.label: Graphify
nodes.rationale: graphify-out/ holds a knowledge graph of the repository. Code files and documents are nodes, imports, calls and references are edges, related nodes are grouped into communities. Asking the graph costs a fraction of the tokens that reading files through repeated searches costs, so agents ask it first.

nodes.label: Installing Graphify
nodes.rationale: Install once with uv tool install graphifyy, or pipx install graphifyy, which provides the graphify command. In Claude Code the /graphify skill wraps the same tool, so there is one underlying tool behind two entry points.

nodes.label: Ask The Graph First
nodes.rationale: Before searching with grep or opening file after file, query the graph. Fall back to grep only when the graph does not answer, or when exact text or line numbers are needed, because those are the two cases a graph cannot serve.

nodes.label: graphify query
nodes.rationale: Walks the graph breadth first and answers a question in words, for example graphify query "how does Today choose each card's next step". Add --dfs to trace one path and --budget N to cap the answer at N tokens, so a search that would otherwise sprawl is bounded.

nodes.label: graphify explain
nodes.rationale: Describes one node and its neighbours, for example graphify explain "nextStepFor".

nodes.label: graphify path
nodes.rationale: Finds how two things connect, for example graphify path "AskPanel" "createAssistant".

nodes.label: graphify affected
nodes.rationale: Lists what a change to something would touch, for example graphify affected "PERSONA_PAGES".

nodes.label: graphify god-nodes
nodes.rationale: Reports the most connected nodes, i.e. the hubs a reader should be careful around when changing something.

nodes.label: GRAPH_REPORT.md
nodes.rationale: graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md is the plain-language overview, for a reader who wants the shape of the repository without running a query.

nodes.label: Keep It Current
nodes.rationale: The graph is committed to the repository, so main must always carry a current one; a stale graph is worse than none because agents trust it over reading the code.

nodes.label: Refresh The Graph As The Last Commit Of Every Pull Request
nodes.rationale: Rebase on main, run graphify update ., and commit graphify-out/. Refreshing inside the pull request keeps main current without an extra commit, which would redeploy the prototype.
nodes.norm_label: refresh the graph as the last commit of every pull request

nodes.label: graphify update .
nodes.rationale: Re-extracts changed code with no model and no key, so the code half of the graph is cheap to keep current on every change.

nodes.label: /graphify . --update Skill For Changed Documents
nodes.rationale: graphify update . covers code only; when a pull request changes documents, also run the /graphify . --update skill, which re-reads changed documents with the model.

nodes.label: Never Merge Graph Files By Hand
nodes.rationale: When two pull requests both change graphify-out/, take either side, run graphify update . again, and commit the result. The graph is a derived artefact, so it is regenerated rather than merged, which cannot produce a graph that matches neither side.
nodes.norm_label: never merge graph files by hand

nodes.label: --force Flag For Node-Count Regression
nodes.rationale: graphify update refuses to write a graph with fewer nodes, a guard against a partial extraction silently shrinking the graph. After a refactor that genuinely deletes code, pass --force to override the guard deliberately.

nodes.label: When To Do A Full Rebuild
nodes.rationale: Rebuild the whole graph with /graphify . instead of updating it when .graphifyignore changes, or when graphify query cannot find code that is known to exist. A changed ignore list or a missing node means the incremental state can no longer be trusted, so a full pass is the only way back to a correct graph.
nodes.norm_label: when to do a full rebuild

nodes.label: .graphifyignore
nodes.rationale: Uses .gitignore syntax and applies on top of .gitignore, so a file is only in the graph if neither list excludes it. When a new kind of generated or binary file appears, add it there.

nodes.label: What The Graph Leaves Out
nodes.rationale: The ignore list keeps out files with no extractable knowledge: images, video and audio, PDFs and Office files, fonts, archives and binaries, Python bytecode, data dumps, the precomputed Jev cache (server/fixtures/jev-cache.json), lockfiles, vendored agent tooling and the graph itself. Excluding them keeps the node count an honest measure of what the repository actually says.
